nameStory: This tiny sea snail gets its species name 'greenlandica' from Greenland, where it was first scientifically described. The genus name 'Boreoscala' means 'northern staircase,' referring to the distinctive ridged spiral shell that looks like a miniature winding staircase climbing toward the Arctic.
description: The Greenland wentletrap is a small marine snail with a beautiful, elongated spiral shell that rarely exceeds half an inch in length. Its creamy white to pale yellow shell features prominent raised ridges (called ribs) that wrap around each whorl like the steps of a spiral staircase. This cold-water species belongs to the wentletrap family, known for their delicate, sculptured shells. Like other wentletraps, it's a predator that feeds on sea anemones and other cnidarians.

idTips.label: Spiral ridges
idTips.description: The shell has distinct raised ribs that spiral around each whorl, feeling rough and bumpy under your fingertip like tiny speed bumps

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small shell, typically 8-12mm long (about the size of your pinky nail), making it easy to overlook among beach debris

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Creamy white to pale yellowish shell that may appear slightly translucent when held up to light

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Tall, narrow conical shell that tapers to a sharp point, resembling a miniature ice cream cone

idTips.label: Opening
idTips.description: Round shell opening (aperture) that feels smooth around the edges, unlike the ridged exterior

habitat: Found in cold North Atlantic waters off the New England coast, typically in deeper offshore areas on sandy or muddy bottoms. Most shells wash ashore after storms on sandy beaches, particularly along the Maine coast and outer Cape Cod. Living specimens are rarely seen by casual beachcombers since they inhabit waters 50+ feet deep.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, appearing bright white and intact among seaweed wrack lines.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season for finding shells, though they're often weathered by this time. Look in the early morning after high tides.
seasonality.fall: Storm seasons bring the best chances of finding recently washed shells, especially after nor'easters along exposed coastlines.
seasonality.winter: Shells become increasingly weathered and rare on beaches, but winter storms occasionally deposit fresh specimens.

funFact: Wentletrap snails can actually 'parachute' through the water by releasing a sticky purple mucus that acts like a balloon, allowing them to drift away from danger or travel between sea anemone colonies to hunt!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small spiral shells, but the prominent raised ribs that wrap around the shell like a spiral staircase are distinctive. Most other small white shells either lack these ridges entirely or have much finer, less prominent ones.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'wentletrap' comes from Dutch 'wenteltrap' meaning 'spiral staircase,' perfectly describing the shell's appearance. These shells were once so prized by collectors that people made fake ones from rice paste to fool buyers in the shell trade.
compareHints: Since this is the only Boreoscala species recorded in New England, compare it to other wentletraps in the region. It's distinguished from the more common Epitonium species by its smaller size and more tightly coiled whorls. The spiral ribs are typically more pronounced and regular than those found on most other regional wentletrap species.
